procedural_history.originating_court: National Consumers Disputes Redressal Commission, New Delhi
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 18.02.2020 of the National Consumers Disputes Redressal Commission, New Delhi in RP No. 156 of 2018
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The National Consumers Disputes Redressal Commission, New Delhi passed an order dated 18.02.2020 in Revision Petition No. 156 of 2018, finding deficiency of service and unfair trade practice.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Yash Raj Films Private Limited appealed to the Supreme Court against the order of the National Consumers Disputes Redressal Commission. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the findings of deficiency of service and unfair trade practice.

directions: we set aside the findings of the impugned order that there is deficiency of service and unfair trade practice, and allow the present appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether there was a deficiency of service on the part of the appellant.

facts: A moviegoer (the complainant) watched a film and discovered that a song used to promote and publicize the movie was not included in the final version shown in the theater.
The complainant alleged that this constituted a 'deficiency' in the entertainment service for which she had paid by purchasing a ticket.
law: The Court referred to the definition of 'deficiency' under Section 2(1)(g) of the Act.

A 'deficiency' is defined as any fault, imperfection, shortcoming, or inadequacy in the quality, nature, and manner of performance that is required to be maintained by law or has been undertaken to be performed in pursuance of a contract.
application: The Court analyzed the basis of the complaint and found that the alleged deficiency arose from the complainant's own expectation that the promotional song would be part of the movie.
The Court determined that this expectation did not stem from a legal requirement or a contractual promise.
It was noted that the essential elements for the formation of a contract, such as an 'offer' or 'proposal' to include the song in the final film, were not satisfied by the promotional trailer.

Therefore, the absence of the song did not meet the legal definition of a 'fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy' in the service provided, as there was no contractual or legal obligation to include it.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the claim of deficiency of service, concluding that the complaint was based on the complainant's personal expectation rather than a breach of any contractual or legal requirement. The Court set aside the lower court's finding and allowed the appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant had indulged in an unfair trade practice.

facts: A moviegoer (complainant) watched a promotional trailer for a movie which included a specific song.
After purchasing a ticket and watching the movie, the complainant discovered that the song from the trailer was not in the final film.
The complainant alleged that this omission constituted an unfair trade practice.
law: The court defined an "unfair trade practice" under Section 2(1)(r) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, as a practice that adopts an unfair or deceptive method to promote a service, including making a false or misleading representation.
For a representation to be considered an unfair trade practice, it must be false in substance and fact.
The court established a test: the discrepancy between the represented fact and the actual fact must be one that a reasonable person would consider material.
The burden of proof is on the complainant to produce cogent evidence to prove that an unfair trade practice occurred.
application: The Court found that the promotional trailer did not fall under any of the specific instances of "unfair method or unfair and deceptive practice" outlined in the Act.
It determined that the trailer did not make a false statement or intend to mislead viewers.
The court noted that the complainant failed to provide any cogent evidence to support the claim of an unfair trade practice, thus not meeting their burden of proof.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the ingredients of an 'unfair trade practice' were not met. Therefore, no case for unfair trade practice was made out, and the court rejected the claim.

arguments.issue_text: Whether there was a deficiency of service on the part of the appellant.
appellant_arguments: A promotional trailer does not constitute an 'offer' or a contractual promise that every element shown will be included in the final film.
The alleged deficiency is based on the complainant's subjective expectation that the song would be in the movie, not on a failure to perform a legal or contractual obligation.
Initially, the District Forum found that there was no relationship of consumer and service provider between the parties.
respondent_arguments: The respondent decided to watch the movie with her family after seeing a song in the promotional trailer, creating an expectation that the song would be part of the film.
The absence of the song in the movie caused disappointment, mental agony, and a feeling of being cheated, which amounts to a deficiency in service.

The State Commission held that entertainment services are covered under the definition of 'service' and the appellant, as a service provider, was deficient for not including the advertised song in the film.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant had indulged in an unfair trade practice.
appellant_arguments: The use of a song in a promotional trailer that is not in the final film is a standard industry practice and not intended to deceive consumers.
A promotional trailer is an advertisement and not a final, binding representation of the film's content, as changes are common during the final editing process.
The act of not including the song from the trailer in the final movie does not rise to the level of a deceptive or unfair trade practice.
respondent_arguments: The appellant engaged in an unfair trade practice by widely circulating a promotional trailer featuring a song to attract audiences, but then not including that song in the actual film.
This practice was deceptive as it misled the respondent and other consumers into watching the movie based on the promotional material.
The State Commission found that the appellant had engaged in an unfair trade practice because the song in the promotional trailer was widely circulated but was not shown in the film.
